summary: Red-flashing light at the outer end of Cleveland's east breakwater, first lit in 1915 and rebuilt in 1918; reachable only by boat.

structures.note: Skeletal steel tower per LighthouseFriends. The light is about 40 feet (12 m) above the water (see light.focal_height_m); the tower's own height is not given.
Air diaphone installed in the enclosure.
D9 steel tower; date of replacement not given in the sources read.

events.note: Group-flashing white light established at the end of the east breakwater extension, June 30, 1915; listed as completed in fiscal 1915 under the name Cleveland East Breakwater East End Light.
Changed to an occulting white electric light, May 1, 1916 (previously acetylene).
Electric siren established at the light, May 15, 1916.
New steel skeletal tower with an enclosure at its top.
Air diaphone replaces the electric siren; operating from July 24, 1918.
New armored submarine cable laid, at a cost LighthouseFriends gives as $6,473.

notes_for_editor: (1) Dates: the USLHS place record gives 1918 as year established and Existing: No. LighthouseFriends and the Commissioner's FY1915 summary give June 30, 1915 for the first light. The 1918 date matches the new steel tower and diaphone. The story states the disagreement and does not pick one silently. The record says kind lighthouse; USLHS says minor aid to navigation. The Ohio Sea Grant guide describes the tower as an active navigational tool, and LighthouseFriends describes the light as still showing its red flash, so the Existing: No entry is treated as out of date. (2) The 1915 plan for shore control (LighthouseFriends) is a plan, not a confirmed arrangement; no source read confirms it was carried out. (3) The armored cable cost ($6,473) comes from LighthouseFriends only. The Commissioner FY1919 summary tables print a Cleveland East Entrance Light Station line, but the cost and work columns are printed in separate blocks and could not be matched to this station by column position, so they are not used. (4) No keeper is named in any source read; the USLHS roster for the place is empty. (5) Current tower's D9 replacement date: not found. Four Chronicling America searches (East Entrance, east breakwater, fog phrases, Ohio papers 1915-1935) returned nothing relevant. (6) Other lights with similar names are separate structures and are not used: Cleveland Harbor Main Entrance and West Pierhead lights; the East Breakwater pierhead light (1911, LighthouseFriends 283, cited once); the Cleveland fog-signal station (1913 appropriation of $17,600 in the Commissioner's report). (7) The 1934 Lighthouse Service Bulletin (p. 13) describes a white light at a Cleveland entrance that is hard to pick out; it does not name the light, so it is not used. (8) The record's Iso R 6s characteristic is kept; the sources describe a red light flashing 3 seconds on and 3 off, which matches. (9) LighthouseFriends is a copyrighted site: the story paraphrases it, and quotations are limited to evidence strings. (10) The focal height of 18 m and range of 7.8 nm are in the record and are not restated here, because no source read in this batch gives them independently (us-lighthouses.com gives a 59 ft focal plane, which agrees, but it is a weak source). (11) Fact-check 2026-10-28: every evidence quote was found in its cached source. The first-light date is now presented as a disagreement in the lead, not as settled. The 1915 date also has Ohio Sea Grant support (the original structure built 1915), which the story now cites. (12) Commissioner FY1915 p. 99: the station name sits in a names column of the summary of construction completed; the story uses only the listing, not a work or cost, so nothing was matched by column position. The FY1916 p. 5 fog-signal sentence and the June 1916 (No. 54) and 3 September 1918 Bulletin dates were checked against the text. (13) The 1915 plan for shore control is reported as a plan; no cited source says it was carried out. (14) LighthouseFriends' 1884 and 1911 passages about keepers at the Cleveland breakwaters (Keeper Goodwin, Assistant Keeper Reed, Frederick T. Hatch) concern other lights and are not used. (15) The light's focal height (about 40 ft, 12 m) was recorded as a tower height in the first draft of this record; it is now light.focal_height_m.
